# Festmaxxing environments

Candidate environments for the product beyond Edinburgh-in-August, scored
against an explicit bar — the **festmaxxing definition** below, extracted from
the owner's stated product direction. The page began as a ranking of festival
*cities* by structural closeness to Edinburgh; the definition generalizes it:
anywhere — festival or not — that is time-boxed, abundant and complex enough
that maximizing a stay there is a genuine optimization problem is a candidate
market. Compiled once, refined in place.

## Key insights

- The festmaxxing bar: week-plus window, options ≫ capacity, real clashes, binding travel, public tickets, same-city recurrence.
- Adelaide is the only real peer, and still under 40% of Edinburgh: 1,648 shows to 4,232.
- Avignon OFF is the closest structural twin — 1,780 open-access shows in 141 theatres inside one walled town.
- Edinburgh has a free official cross-festival listings API. No other festival city found has an equivalent.
- Fashion week has the shape but no market: the real catalogue is invitation-only, and every show happens exactly once.
- The Olympics sells 9.5m public tickets across 767 sessions — then moves cities, so a planner's data dies every four years.
- Open per-event access is the rarest dimension at mega-events; where it meets an annual anchor, a planner's data compounds.

## The festmaxxing bar

The owner's product direction (2026-09-01): the next evolution of EdFringeNow
is **the planning tool for festival fanatics** — people who travel to an event
to maximize their time there, weaving in time off, food and excursions, and who
need a tool *because the environment is complex*. Handling that complexity is
the reason to use the product; the owner's word for the behaviour is
**festmaxxing**. Three characteristics name where such a tool matters — **time
limitation, complexity, abundance** — and they unpack into eight testable
dimensions.

**The shape** — is a stay there an optimization problem at all?

1. **Time-boxed window** — fixed dates, roughly a week or longer. A weekend
   plans itself; a longer run forces choices about *which days to even be
   there*. (Owner: don't focus on the quick 4-day events.)
2. **Abundance** — the catalogue far exceeds one person's capacity; even a
   maximal plan samples a fraction of it.
3. **Simultaneity** — many options run at once, so every pick forecloses
   others; conflicts are the norm, not the exception.
4. **Venue spread** — venues scattered enough that travel time is a binding
   constraint; a plan that ignores the map is infeasible, not merely
   suboptimal.
5. **Repeat chances** — items recur inside the window, turning "which do I
   drop" into "which order do I go". This is the fringe-shaped vs
   showcase-shaped axis worked through on
   [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md); both
   shapes are planning problems, but recurrence is what makes the product
   *optimization* rather than triage.

**The qualifiers** — can our product serve it, and keep serving it?

6. **Open per-event access** — a member of the public can buy a ticket (or
   book a slot) to a specific item. Badge-only, invite-only and
   one-wristband-for-everything environments can have the shape yet offer no
   bookable unit for a planner to link to.
7. **Anchored recurrence** — annual (or a fixed cycle) in the same city and
   largely the same venues, so venue data, travel matrices and source
   integrations compound year over year instead of resetting. (Owner: "very
   important to know if a festival is an annual event in the same city/venues
   … or a one-off.")

**The enrichment axis** — the "time off" half of festmaxxing.

8. **City context** — real non-event material around the event (food,
   excursions, rest), because a festmaxxing plan is a *stay*, not a bare
   schedule. Where each city publishes that layer is
   [city-context-sources/](../city-context-sources/README.md)'s subject.

Dimensions 1–5 decide whether the environment *has* the problem; 6–7 decide
whether a product can serve it; 8 decides how rich the plan can be. The tiers
below apply the bar to every candidate this page has gathered — festivals and,
since 2026-09-01, non-festival environments that share the shape.

**The shape already sells.** The nearest commercial proof that people pay for
constrained-itinerary optimization is not a festival product at all:
[TouringPlans](https://touringplans.com/) sells Walt Disney World visitors
step-by-step touring plans, crowd calendars and live wait-time re-optimization
for a **$24.97/year** subscription. A theme park fails the bar's first
dimension — the park is continuous, and the time box is the visitor's own
trip — but it holds the seventh absolutely, and that permanent anchor is what
makes the model work: decades of wait-time data on the same rides. The lesson
cuts both ways for a festival planner: the Fringe has the anchor, but only a
25-day season to sell against.

## What "another Edinburgh" actually means

Edinburgh's August is not one festival. Eleven major festivals share the city
across the year, and in August the Fringe (7–31 Aug 2026), the International
Festival (7–30), the Tattoo (7–29), the Art Festival (14–30), the Book Festival
(15–30) and the International Film Festival (13–19) overlap, with the densest
window around 14–25 August.

Underneath that, the thing that actually generates the overwhelm is the Fringe's
**open-access** model: anyone who finds a room and pays a registration fee is
listed, so supply is uncapped and the city converts itself into venues. Scale
figures for the Fringe itself live on
[edinburgh-market-and-audience/](../edinburgh-market-and-audience/README.md) — 4,232 shows across 306
venues, 2.81m tickets, both final delivered 2026 figures.

Three distinct mechanisms produce an Edinburgh-shaped city, and they matter
separately because each implies a different data and product problem:

1. **Open access** — uncapped supply, one registration fee, thousands of parallel
   runs. This is the mechanism EdFringeNow is built against.
2. **A curated core with an unofficial "off"** — a ticketed official programme
   plus a sprawling satellite ecosystem the official body does not list.
3. **A festival *season*** — many discrete, separately-run festivals stacked
   back-to-back in one city, rather than one festival with thousands of shows.

A fourth, weaker pattern — **long temporary exhibition runs** (biennials) — makes
a city swarm without producing a scheduling problem, because a months-long
exhibition has no performance times to clash. Non-festival environments reach
the bar through mechanisms of their own (a convention's parallel programming
tracks, a mega-event's session grid); the bar, not the mechanism, is what
qualifies a candidate.

## The candidates, scored

Every candidate keeps its mechanism label and gets a verdict against the bar.
One standing caution applies to the whole list: scale figures are cited from
programme-launch press unless marked delivered — the launch-vs-delivered trap
recorded in the 2026-08-09 correction below.

### Clears the bar

#### Adelaide — the only peer by scale

Adelaide Fringe is the world's second-largest annual arts festival and is
explicitly open access ("welcomes anyone with an event to participate"). The 2026
edition ran **20 February – 22 March** with **1,648 shows across 562 venues** and
about **1,083,000 tickets** sold, part of more than six million attendances at
ticketed and free events.

It shares the surrounding-cluster property too: the Adelaide Festival, WOMADelaide
and Writers' Week run alongside it, which is why locals call the period "Mad
March."

Two structural differences that matter to the product:

- **It is not one calendar month.** 20 Feb – 22 Mar spans two months. The
  planner's calendar axis is a single month.
- **562 venues to Edinburgh's 258**, in a city with a far less compact core —
  travel-time estimation is doing more work there, not less. On the bar: venue
  spread (dimension 4) binds *harder* than in Edinburgh.

#### Avignon — the closest structural twin

Avignon in July is the same *shape* as Edinburgh in August: a curated Festival
d'Avignon ("the IN") plus the open-access **Festival OFF**, inside a small walled
medieval town. The 60th OFF (**4–25 July 2026**) carried **1,780 shows in 141
theatres**, roughly **27,000 performances**, around 1,250 performances a day, from
~1,600 companies (about 90% French). Average auditorium fill was **54%** —
the same "too much supply chasing too little attention" economics as the Fringe.

If any city is EdFringeNow's second market on structure alone, it is this one.
The blocker is not the bar — every dimension clears — it is that the entire
corpus is in French.

#### The rest of the clear tier

- **Perth, Australia — FRINGE WORLD** (Jan–Feb; open access). The third-largest
  fringe on the planet: **600+ shows across 110 venues** advertised ahead of the
  2026 edition (21 Jan–15 Feb 2026), ~3,000 artists, off **256,000 tickets**
  sold in 2025. That 2026 edition has since run and closed (this repo's clock
  is now 2 Aug 2026): its own final report counts **599 events**, more than
  3,000 artists, **nearly 500,000 attendees**, and **$10.9m spent at the Box
  Office** ($8.34m paid to artists and venues) — up from 2025's 570 events /
  492,369 attendees / $10.78m box office. Note "attendees" and "tickets sold"
  are not the same metric (the 256,000 figure is a narrower paid-ticket count);
  both are kept because neither source reconciles them into one number.
- **Brighton, UK** (1–31 May; open access). Around **400,000 in-person
  attendances**, with over 30% of events from Brighton & Hove companies. English
  language, UK ticketing conventions — the cheapest possible second market.
  Comedy share and its open Eventotron API are on
  [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md).
- **Melbourne — MICF** (Mar–Apr; open registration). The strongest
  fringe-shaped candidate found anywhere outside the fringe network itself:
  803 shows, 9,164 performances, 26 days, with open JSON endpoints.
  [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md) owns the
  detail; it sits in this tier on every dimension.
- **Montreal in July** (festival season). Festival International de Jazz de
  Montréal (25 Jun – 4 Jul 2026) puts **350+ shows** and 3,000 performers in
  front of a claimed 2m+ guests; Just For Laughs (15–26 Jul 2026) runs **250
  shows across 25 downtown venues** and 800+ artists **in both official
  languages**, and the Fantasia film festival overlaps JFL for eleven shared
  days. Concentrated in the Quartier des Spectacles, so reachability is real.
  Bilingual by default — the first candidate that forces the localization
  question. On the bar it clears as a *stacked season* rather than one
  festival, which multiplies the data-source cost (each festival is separately
  run). (Corrected 2026-09-01: this entry called JFL "the world's largest
  comedy festival". That label is JFL marketing that survives on attendance
  counting its free outdoor crowds; by ticketed shows it is roughly a third of
  Melbourne's 803, and the company behind it went through 2024 receivership
  and a 2024 cancellation before its 2026 relaunch — see
  [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md), which now
  owns the comedy-festival detail for this and every other comedy entry.)
- **Makhanda (Grahamstown), South Africa — National Arts Festival** (late
  June–July; open-access fringe beside a curated core). **270+ productions** on
  the main programme in 2026 plus a Fringe of **200+ new works**, in a town
  small enough that the visitor-to-resident ratio may be the most extreme of
  any candidate here. Clears the bar at the small end — abundance is relative
  to the visitor's capacity, and eleven days of ~470 productions clears it.
- **Sibiu, Romania — FITS** (19–28 June 2026; curated season). **800+ events**
  in ten days in a small old town; one of Europe's largest performing-arts
  festivals. Curated rather than open access, but 80 events a day produces
  real simultaneity — the mechanism differs, the bar clears.
- **The film festivals that clear it** — Berlinale above all (274 films, each
  screened up to five times, public tickets €9–15), then TIFF and MIFF.
  [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md)'s film
  adjacency owns the detail and citations; they belong on this page's map
  because each is an anchored, publicly-ticketed, repeat-screening city event.
- **Miami Art Week / Art Basel Miami Beach** (December; curated core + off —
  promoted from this page's unassessed tail 2026-09-01). One fixed week (2–9
  Dec in 2024) with **20+ art fairs and 1,200+ galleries in aggregate**
  scattered across Miami Beach, Wynwood, the Design District, Downtown and
  beyond; the anchor fair alone carried 280+ galleries with public day
  tickets at $85. Each fair is separately publicly ticketed and open daily
  through the week — sequencing, not triage — and metro traffic makes travel
  the binding constraint. The strongest non-theatre clear found:
  structurally a fringe whose shows are fairs.
- **Open House Festival, London** (September; a city-wide open week). **Over
  800 free open days and events across all 33 boroughs** in 9 days (12–20
  Sep 2026, 35th edition): drop-in for most buildings, per-item booked slots
  for the popular ones — free, but a real scarce-slot race (bookings open
  ~3.5 weeks out and the hot buildings go in minutes). Venue spread is the
  most extreme on this page. One caveat keeps it at the tier's edge: many
  buildings open on a single day of the nine, so part of the catalogue is
  triage rather than optimization (dimension 5, partial).

### Near misses — one dimension short

- **Milan — Salone del Mobile / Fuorisalone** (April; curated core + off). The
  purest non-theatre version of the Edinburgh dynamic: a ticketed trade fair at
  Rho with 1,900+ exhibitors, plus **1,100+ events listed on the official
  Fuorisalone guide (1,300+ across the city) spread over 16 districts** and
  **500,000+ visitors**. Brera alone carried 320 events across 217 showrooms.
  Installations run for the week rather than to performance times, so
  simultaneity (dimension 3) never bites: the *scheduling* problem is weaker
  than the *reachability* problem — which is the half of the product the Now
  page serves.
- **Charleston, SC — Spoleto Festival USA / Piccolo Spoleto** (late May–June;
  curated core + open companion). Piccolo Spoleto 2026 offered **250 events**,
  190 of them produced by independent arts and community groups, 113 free — a
  deliberately open companion to a curated core, at a scale where a planner is
  plausible but not urgent. Short of the bar on abundance (dimension 2).
- **Toronto, Canada** (30 Jun – 12 Jul 2026; lottery-selected fringe). **123
  shows**, selected by *lottery* rather than pure open access — a different
  supply mechanism, and small enough that overwhelm is not really the user's
  problem. Short on abundance (dimension 2).
- **Galway, Ireland — GIAF** (13–26 July 2026; curated season). Fourteen days,
  audiences well in excess of 200,000, in a small city fully consumed by it.
  Programme size unassessed — provisionally here until a show count is cited.
- **Israel's cinematheque festivals — Jerusalem, Docaviv (Tel Aviv), Haifa**
  (July / late May–June / the Sukkot holiday week; curated film festivals).
  All three clear seven dimensions: 8–11 day windows, 120–200+ films each
  screened 2–3 times, four to five parallel halls, open per-screening
  tickets at ₪43–49, and 28–43 year anchors in the same cities. What each
  misses is venue spread (dimension 4): everything concentrates in one
  cinematheque hub, so travel never binds and daily volume tops out near 28
  screenings — a planner is useful there, not indispensable. Detail and
  citations on [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md)'s
  film adjacency, extended to Israel 2026-09-01.
- **Gen Con, Indianapolis** (July–Aug; convention — badge plus per-event
  tickets). The closest non-festival analogue found anywhere: **nearly
  30,000 unique ticketed events in four days** for ~72,000 attendees (2025,
  sold out), every event booked individually on top of a ~$155 badge with $2
  generic tickets as standby — the Fringe's model with a cover charge,
  anchored to Indianapolis since 2003 and contracted there through 2030.
  Event registration is itself a famous scarcity rush. What it misses: the
  window (4 days, dimension 1) and venue spread (one connected downtown
  campus — walking, not travel, is the constraint; dimension 4).
- **NYC Restaurant Week** (twice yearly; the reservation-as-ticket model).
  Nearly **600 restaurants across all five boroughs** on $30/$45/$60
  prix-fixe menus for four weeks (summer 2025), booked through OpenTable —
  a genuinely scarce per-item public slot that repeats daily through the
  window. Misses on intensity (dimension 3): two or three meal slots a day
  is planning, but rarely *conflict* — and the catalogue is the city's
  ordinary restaurant scene, already served by incumbent dining tools.

### Fails the bar, instructively

- **Salzburg, Austria** (17 Jul – 30 Aug 2026). **208 performances**
  announced for 2026; the delivered 2025 season was **174 performances over
  45 days at 16 venues, at 98.4% occupancy** — roughly four a day, so an
  evening rarely forecloses more than one alternative. The town is
  overwhelmed, but the programme is curated, expensive and near-sold-out — a
  season you *book*, not a schedule you optimize. The boundary case this
  page keeps on purpose: *city swarming* alone fails abundance and
  simultaneity (dimensions 2–3), even with the deepest anchor on this page
  (annual in one town since 1920).
- **Venice — Biennale Arte** (9 May – 22 Nov 2026). **100 national
  participations** — 29 in the Giardini, 25 in the Arsenale and **46 scattered
  across the city** — plus **31 collateral events**. A months-long run means
  opening hours, not performance times: fails time-boxing (1) and simultaneity
  (3) at once. **Kassel — Documenta** (every five years, 100 days) fails the
  cadence half of recurrence; the roving **Manifesta** fails the anchor half.
- **Cannes**, **SXSW Austin** (March). Both convert a city into temporary
  venues at high density with genuine clash-resolution problems, but both are
  trade/badge-driven rather than public-audience-driven — failing open access
  (dimension 6) — and SXSW already ships its own scheduling tool.
- **Fashion week — Paris, Milan, New York, London** (the owner's direct
  question, 2026-09-01). It has festival *shape*: a fixed week per city
  (NYFW's February 2026 official calendar ran 6 days with 60+ shows and
  presentations; Paris womenswear runs 9 days with ~68 shows and 33
  presentations), venues scattered across the city, twice-plus a year in
  the same capitals. It fails the bar twice over. **The real catalogue is
  invitation- and accreditation-only** — runway seats go to press, buyers
  and clients, and what the public can buy (Runway 7-style independent
  showcases in New York, London's £135 public-ticket experiment of 2019,
  Copenhagen's partly-open schedule) is a parallel shadow programme, not
  the shows that matter (dimension 6). And **every show happens exactly
  once** (dimension 5), so even for insiders it is triage, not
  optimization. The scheduling pain is real; the bookable market is absent.
- **The Summer Olympics** (the owner's other direct question; mega-event).
  Paris 2024 is the strongest possible showing for the shape: 17 days, **767
  ticketed sessions across 35 venues** (~20 in and around one city), **9.5
  million tickets sold** to the general public from €24, with an official
  face-value resale app — better-behaved public access than most festivals,
  plus genuine abundance and binding travel. It still fails the two
  dimensions a planning product compounds on: sessions never repeat (the
  100m final does not recur on Tuesday; dimension 5), and **the host city
  rotates every four years** (dimension 7), so venue data, travel matrices
  and source work are worthless at the next edition. A real planning
  market — for exactly one summer per city. FIFA World Cup 2026 doubles the
  failure: 104 matches across 16 cities in three countries, with flights as
  the travel legs.
- **The badge-and-queue worlds — San Diego Comic-Con, CES** (conventions).
  SDCC: ~130,000 attendees and dozens of parallel programming tracks, but
  **one badge and then first-come queueing** — no per-item slot exists to
  book (Hall H is famously camped overnight), so the optimization is real
  but unbookable (dimension 6), and its fan-run schedule guides are the
  community routing around that. CES: 4,100+ exhibitors across two Las
  Vegas campuses far enough apart that navigation is a product feature —
  but trade-only badges, closed to the public (dimension 6 again, from the
  other side).
- **Burning Man** (temporary city). Nine days, one rebuilt city, and a
  community-published catalogue of **4,300+ participant-run events** (the
  2018 Playa Events count) — proof that an event catalogue emerges wherever
  abundance meets a time box, even with no commerce at all. It fails on
  access (one $550+ ticket covers everything; per-event ticketing is
  unticketable by ideology; dimension 6) and on city context (dimension 8:
  there is no surrounding city — food and rest are things you truck in).

### The unassessed tail

The World Fringe network holds 300+ fringes worldwide (Perth's own materials
say 400+), and the tail is thin — only three sell more than 250,000 tickets.
In the network and unassessed here: **Prague**, **Dublin**, **Winnipeg**,
**Orlando**, **Minnesota**, **Wellington**, **Camden**, **Melbourne Fringe**.

The cross-cutting finding from scoring the non-festival world (2026-09-01):
**open per-event access is the definition's rarest dimension.** Big
real-world events default to allocating scarcity by badge, invitation or
queue; genuinely bookable per-item inventory is what festivals proper, Gen
Con, the art fairs, Open House and restaurant weeks share. And it is the
pairing of that access with an annual anchor that makes a planning product's
data investment compound — where either half fails, the planning problem
still exists but belongs to insiders (fashion week, CES), queue-campers
(SDCC), or a single summer (each Olympics).
# City context sources — finding everything else that's on

Where "what else is going on in this city" gets published, and how a product
can read it. This page exists on the owner's direction (2026-09-01): a
festival visitor also wants the rest of the city — other events that week,
attractions, markets — and the wiki's job is **not** to hold any particular
weekend's events but to hold **the sources**: which publications, feeds and
APIs carry a city's non-festival goings-on, per festival city, and how
machine-readable each is. Scoped to the cities of the longer festivals
([festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md)'s
fringe-shaped tier), not the weekend showcases. Edinburgh's own August
*festival* cluster is [edinburgh-festival-season/](../edinburgh-festival-season/README.md)'s;
this page is about everything those pages don't list. Compiled once, refined
in place.

Every claim below was verified by direct fetch on 2026-09-01 unless marked
as a search-attributed claim; "closed" verdicts name what was actually
probed.

## Key insights

- Events listings are a per-country licensed market: Data Thistle (UK), ATDW (Australia), Eventfinda (NZ) cover our cities in one API each.
- Montreal is the outlier: the city's own open-data portal publishes its events calendar as CSV/GeoJSON, refreshed daily.
- Tourism-board sites have no APIs — but their event detail pages carry schema.org JSON-LD, so one parser covers every city.
- The open-API era is over: Eventbrite killed public event search in 2020, Songkick takes no new keys, Fever bought DICE.
- Ticketmaster Discovery and Skiddle are the free keyed baseline — geo-searchable, 5k calls/day, with a ticketed-music skew.
- Attractions are solved free: OSM Overpass plus Wikidata; Viator's no-gate affiliate tier adds bookable tours with commission.
- Data Thistle is competitor and supplier at once: it sells the listings feed the UK's own tourism boards run on.

## The source classes

**1. Tourism-board (DMO) event calendars** are the best human-curated
coverage of "everything else in town" — promoters submit events directly
(every DMO probed has a submit flow) — and the weakest machine surface: none
probed offers a documented API. The verified pattern across seven DMOs:
index pages carry only site-level JSON-LD, but **event detail pages carry
full schema.org `Event` markup** (wellingtonnz.com's detail pages have
`MusicEvent` with `startDate` and `Place`), so the generic integration is a
sitemap crawl plus a JSON-LD parse of detail pages — one parser for every
city. Some have undocumented JSON backends (aucklandnz.com calls its own
`/api/events/get`); some are bot-hostile (visitmelbourne.com 403s
non-browsers; What's On Melbourne renders client-side).

**2. City open-data portals** carry attractions/POI and event
*infrastructure*, not live listings — with one exception worth building on:
[Montreal's "Événements publics" dataset](https://donnees.montreal.ca/)
(CKAN, API works unauthenticated) is the city's own calendar as
CSV/GeoJSON — date, event type, audience, cost, location — last modified
the day it was checked, i.e. maintained daily. Melbourne's Opendatasoft
portal (239 datasets, open API) has venues, landmarks and event *permits*
but no calendar; Edinburgh's legacy portal was unreachable (502) and its
live ArcGIS portal is spatial-only.

**3. Commercial listings media** (Time Out, The Skinny, Broadsheet, The
List's consumer site) are editorial and scrape-only; no licensing program
surfaced for Time Out. The class that matters sits behind them:

**4. Licensed events-data suppliers — the class the UK actually runs on.**
[Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/) (The List's data arm,
Edinburgh-based) claims over half a million future performances UK-wide and
publishes a [documented Publishing API](https://api.datathistle.com/) —
free registration, event/place/schedule/performance model **with
per-performance prices and booking links** — and its named clients include
VisitScotland, Visit Brighton, Visit Liverpool and Transport for Edinburgh,
via the Simpleview CMS the DMOs run on. One integration would cover
Edinburgh, Brighton and Leicester at once — and its data model is
structurally a superset of what EdFringeNow already stores. Australia's
equivalent is national and official: the
[Australian Tourism Data Warehouse ATLAS API](https://developer.atdw.com.au/)
(products *and events*, feeding the state DMO sites; distributor
registration A$660 once-off with a 30-day trial, per its own FAQ) — one
paid integration covers Melbourne and Adelaide. New Zealand's is
[Eventfinda's API](https://www.eventfinda.co.nz/api/v2/index) (free key by
application, display-only licence with attribution) covering Auckland and
Wellington.

**5. Ticketing-platform discovery APIs** — the survivors and the dead:
[Ticketmaster Discovery](https://developer.ticketmaster.com/products-and-docs/apis/discovery-api/v2/)
(free key, 5,000 calls/day, geo+date+venue search, global) and
[Skiddle](https://github.com/Skiddle/web-api) (UK; free key, lat/long/radius,
event codes including COMEDY and EXHIB) are real and open.
**Eventbrite has no public discovery API** — the public event search was
removed in February 2020 and the API is org-scoped now; **Songkick** takes
no new API applications (commercial licence ~$500/month per its support
pages); **DICE** is partner-only and was acquired by **Fever** (itself
closed) in June 2025; **Bandsintown** is artist-scoped — the wrong shape
for city-wide discovery. Universe has an open GraphQL API but niche
inventory.

**6. Event-intelligence aggregators**: [PredictHQ](https://docs.predicthq.com/)
sells exactly "all events in a city" (free tier exists; real pricing
negotiated) but is built for demand forecasting — whether its licence
permits consumer republishing is unverified and decides whether it is
usable at all. SeatGeek's Platform API is real, free-keyed, US-leaning.

**7. Attractions, as distinct from events**: the free, licence-clean base
layer is [OpenStreetMap's Overpass API](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Overpass_API)
(`tourism=attraction|museum|viewpoint`, opening hours where mapped) joined
with [Wikidata's SPARQL endpoint](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:SPARQL_query_service)
(CC0 entities, coordinates, images, Wikipedia links) — the "free hour near
me" gazetteer, and the machine version of the hand-curated list
[edinburgh-festival-season/](../edinburgh-festival-season/README.md) said couldn't exist as a
feed. For *bookable* attractions,
[Viator's Partner API basic-access tier is free with no pre-authorization](https://docs.viator.com/partner-api/technical/)
(search, availability, pricing, commission on referred bookings) — which
also plugs into the affiliate lane
[competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md)'s revenue
analysis found empty among rivals; GetYourGuide gates its API behind 100k
monthly visits and Tiqets behind partner contact; Google Places is paid
per-request; Atlas Obscura is bot-blocked with no API.

## Per-city: what a product would actually read

| City (festival, window) | Best sources | Machine access |
|---|---|---|
| Edinburgh (Fringe, Aug) | Data Thistle API;

1	# Festmaxxing environments
2	
3	Candidate environments for the product beyond Edinburgh-in-August, scored
4	against an explicit bar — the **festmaxxing definition** below, extracted from
5	the owner's stated product direction. The page began as a ranking of festival
6	*cities* by structural closeness to Edinburgh; the definition generalizes it:
7	anywhere — festival or not — that is time-boxed, abundant and complex enough
8	that maximizing a stay there is a genuine optimization problem is a candidate
9	market. Compiled once, refined in place.
10	
11	## Key insights
12	
13	- The festmaxxing bar: week-plus window, options ≫ capacity, real clashes, binding travel, public tickets, same-city recurrence.
14	- Adelaide is the only real peer, and still under 40% of Edinburgh: 1,648 shows to 4,232.
15	- Avignon OFF is the closest structural twin — 1,780 open-access shows in 141 theatres inside one walled town.
16	- Edinburgh has a free official cross-festival listings API. No other festival city found has an equivalent.
17	- Fashion week has the shape but no market: the real catalogue is invitation-only, and every show happens exactly once.
18	- The Olympics sells 9.5m public tickets across 767 sessions — then moves cities, so a planner's data dies every four years.
19	- Open per-event access is the rarest dimension at mega-events; where it meets an annual anchor, a planner's data compounds.
20	
21	## The festmaxxing bar
22	
23	The owner's product direction (2026-09-01): the next evolution of EdFringeNow
24	is **the planning tool for festival fanatics** — people who travel to an event
25	to maximize their time there, weaving in time off, food and excursions, and who
26	need a tool *because the environment is complex*. Handling that complexity is
27	the reason to use the product; the owner's word for the behaviour is
28	**festmaxxing**. Three characteristics name where such a tool matters — **time
29	limitation, complexity, abundance** — and they unpack into eight testable
30	dimensions.
31	
32	**The shape** — is a stay there an optimization problem at all?
33	
34	1. **Time-boxed window** — fixed dates, roughly a week or longer. A weekend
35	   plans itself; a longer run forces choices about *which days to even be
36	   there*. (Owner: don't focus on the quick 4-day events.)
37	2. **Abundance** — the catalogue far exceeds one person's capacity; even a
38	   maximal plan samples a fraction of it.
39	3. **Simultaneity** — many options run at once, so every pick forecloses
40	   others; conflicts are the norm, not the exception.
41	4. **Venue spread** — venues scattered enough that travel time is a binding
42	   constraint; a plan that ignores the map is infeasible, not merely
43	   suboptimal.
44	5. **Repeat chances** — items recur inside the window, turning "which do I
45	   drop" into "which order do I go". This is the fringe-shaped vs
46	   showcase-shaped axis worked through on
47	   [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md); both
48	   shapes are planning problems, but recurrence is what makes the product
49	   *optimization* rather than triage.
50	
51	**The qualifiers** — can our product serve it, and keep serving it?
52	
53	6. **Open per-event access** — a member of the public can buy a ticket (or
54	   book a slot) to a specific item. Badge-only, invite-only and
55	   one-wristband-for-everything environments can have the shape yet offer no
56	   bookable unit for a planner to link to.
57	7. **Anchored recurrence** — annual (or a fixed cycle) in the same city and
58	   largely the same venues, so venue data, travel matrices and source
59	   integrations compound year over year instead of resetting. (Owner: "very
60	   important to know if a festival is an annual event in the same city/venues
61	   … or a one-off.")
62	
63	**The enrichment axis** — the "time off" half of festmaxxing.
64	
65	8. **City context** — real non-event material around the event (food,
66	   excursions, rest), because a festmaxxing plan is a *stay*, not a bare
67	   schedule. Where each city publishes that layer is
68	   [city-context-sources/](../city-context-sources/README.md)'s subject.
69	
70	Dimensions 1–5 decide whether the environment *has* the problem; 6–7 decide
71	whether a product can serve it; 8 decides how rich the plan can be. The tiers
72	below apply the bar to every candidate this page has gathered — festivals and,
73	since 2026-09-01, non-festival environments that share the shape.
74	
75	**The shape already sells.** The nearest commercial proof that people pay for
76	constrained-itinerary optimization is not a festival product at all:
77	[TouringPlans](https://touringplans.com/) sells Walt Disney World visitors
78	step-by-step touring plans, crowd calendars and live wait-time re-optimization
79	for a **$24.97/year** subscription. A theme park fails the bar's first
80	dimension — the park is continuous, and the time box is the visitor's own
81	trip — but it holds the seventh absolutely, and that permanent anchor is what
82	makes the model work: decades of wait-time data on the same rides. The lesson
83	cuts both ways for a festival planner: the Fringe has the anchor, but only a
84	25-day season to sell against.
85	
86	## What "another Edinburgh" actually means
87	
88	Edinburgh's August is not one festival. Eleven major festivals share the city
89	across the year, and in August the Fringe (7–31 Aug 2026), the International
90	Festival (7–30), the Tattoo (7–29), the Art Festival (14–30), the Book Festival
91	(15–30) and the International Film Festival (13–19) overlap, with the densest
92	window around 14–25 August.
93	
94	Underneath that, the thing that actually generates the overwhelm is the Fringe's
95	**open-access** model: anyone who finds a room and pays a registration fee is
96	listed, so supply is uncapped and the city converts itself into venues. Scale
97	figures for the Fringe itself live on
98	[edinburgh-market-and-audience/](../edinburgh-market-and-audience/README.md) — 4,232 shows across 306
99	venues, 2.81m tickets, both final delivered 2026 figures.
100	
101	Three distinct mechanisms produce an Edinburgh-shaped city, and they matter
102	separately because each implies a different data and product problem:
103	
104	1. **Open access** — uncapped supply, one registration fee, thousands of parallel
105	   runs. This is the mechanism EdFringeNow is built against.
106	2. **A curated core with an unofficial "off"** — a ticketed official programme
107	   plus a sprawling satellite ecosystem the official body does not list.
108	3. **A festival *season*** — many discrete, separately-run festivals stacked
109	   back-to-back in one city, rather than one festival with thousands of shows.
110	
111	A fourth, weaker pattern — **long temporary exhibition runs** (biennials) — makes
112	a city swarm without producing a scheduling problem, because a months-long
113	exhibition has no performance times to clash. Non-festival environments reach
114	the bar through mechanisms of their own (a convention's parallel programming
115	tracks, a mega-event's session grid); the bar, not the mechanism, is what
116	qualifies a candidate.
117	
118	## The candidates, scored
119	
120	Every candidate keeps its mechanism label and gets a verdict against the bar.
121	One standing caution applies to the whole list: scale figures are cited from
122	programme-launch press unless marked delivered — the launch-vs-delivered trap
123	recorded in the 2026-08-09 correction below.
124	
125	### Clears the bar
126	
127	#### Adelaide — the only peer by scale
128	
129	Adelaide Fringe is the world's second-largest annual arts festival and is
130	explicitly open access ("welcomes anyone with an event to participate"). The 2026
131	edition ran **20 February – 22 March** with **1,648 shows across 562 venues** and
132	about **1,083,000 tickets** sold, part of more than six million attendances at
133	ticketed and free events.
134	
135	It shares the surrounding-cluster property too: the Adelaide Festival, WOMADelaide
136	and Writers' Week run alongside it, which is why locals call the period "Mad
137	March."
138	
139	Two structural differences that matter to the product:
140	
141	- **It is not one calendar month.** 20 Feb – 22 Mar spans two months. The
142	  planner's calendar axis is a single month.
143	- **562 venues to Edinburgh's 258**, in a city with a far less compact core —
144	  travel-time estimation is doing more work there, not less. On the bar: venue
145	  spread (dimension 4) binds *harder* than in Edinburgh.
146	
147	#### Avignon — the closest structural twin
148	
149	Avignon in July is the same *shape* as Edinburgh in August: a curated Festival
150	d'Avignon ("the IN") plus the open-access **Festival OFF**, inside a small walled
151	medieval town. The 60th OFF (**4–25 July 2026**) carried **1,780 shows in 141
152	theatres**, roughly **27,000 performances**, around 1,250 performances a day, from
153	~1,600 companies (about 90% French). Average auditorium fill was **54%** —
154	the same "too much supply chasing too little attention" economics as the Fringe.
155	
156	If any city is EdFringeNow's second market on structure alone, it is this one.
157	The blocker is not the bar — every dimension clears — it is that the entire
158	corpus is in French.
159	
160	#### The rest of the clear tier
161	
162	- **Perth, Australia — FRINGE WORLD** (Jan–Feb; open access). The third-largest
163	  fringe on the planet: **600+ shows across 110 venues** advertised ahead of the
164	  2026 edition (21 Jan–15 Feb 2026), ~3,000 artists, off **256,000 tickets**
165	  sold in 2025. That 2026 edition has since run and closed (this repo's clock
166	  is now 2 Aug 2026): its own final report counts **599 events**, more than
167	  3,000 artists, **nearly 500,000 attendees**, and **$10.9m spent at the Box
168	  Office** ($8.34m paid to artists and venues) — up from 2025's 570 events /
169	  492,369 attendees / $10.78m box office. Note "attendees" and "tickets sold"
170	  are not the same metric (the 256,000 figure is a narrower paid-ticket count);
171	  both are kept because neither source reconciles them into one number.
172	- **Brighton, UK** (1–31 May; open access). Around **400,000 in-person
173	  attendances**, with over 30% of events from Brighton & Hove companies. English
174	  language, UK ticketing conventions — the cheapest possible second market.
175	  Comedy share and its open Eventotron API are on
176	  [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md).
177	- **Melbourne — MICF** (Mar–Apr; open registration). The strongest
178	  fringe-shaped candidate found anywhere outside the fringe network itself:
179	  803 shows, 9,164 performances, 26 days, with open JSON endpoints.
180	  [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md) owns the
181	  detail; it sits in this tier on every dimension.
182	- **Montreal in July** (festival season). Festival International de Jazz de
183	  Montréal (25 Jun – 4 Jul 2026) puts **350+ shows** and 3,000 performers in
184	  front of a claimed 2m+ guests; Just For Laughs (15–26 Jul 2026) runs **250
185	  shows across 25 downtown venues** and 800+ artists **in both official
186	  languages**, and the Fantasia film festival overlaps JFL for eleven shared
187	  days. Concentrated in the Quartier des Spectacles, so reachability is real.
188	  Bilingual by default — the first candidate that forces the localization
189	  question. On the bar it clears as a *stacked season* rather than one
190	  festival, which multiplies the data-source cost (each festival is separately
191	  run). (Corrected 2026-09-01: this entry called JFL "the world's largest
192	  comedy festival". That label is JFL marketing that survives on attendance
193	  counting its free outdoor crowds; by ticketed shows it is roughly a third of
194	  Melbourne's 803, and the company behind it went through 2024 receivership
195	  and a 2024 cancellation before its 2026 relaunch — see
196	  [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md), which now
197	  owns the comedy-festival detail for this and every other comedy entry.)
198	- **Makhanda (Grahamstown), South Africa — National Arts Festival** (late
199	  June–July; open-access fringe beside a curated core). **270+ productions** on
200	  the main programme in 2026 plus a Fringe of **200+ new works**, in a town
201	  small enough that the visitor-to-resident ratio may be the most extreme of
202	  any candidate here. Clears the bar at the small end — abundance is relative
203	  to the visitor's capacity, and eleven days of ~470 productions clears it.
204	- **Sibiu, Romania — FITS** (19–28 June 2026; curated season). **800+ events**
205	  in ten days in a small old town; one of Europe's largest performing-arts
206	  festivals. Curated rather than open access, but 80 events a day produces
207	  real simultaneity — the mechanism differs, the bar clears.
208	- **The film festivals that clear it** — Berlinale above all (274 films, each
209	  screened up to five times, public tickets €9–15), then TIFF and MIFF.
210	  [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md)'s film
211	  adjacency owns the detail and citations; they belong on this page's map
212	  because each is an anchored, publicly-ticketed, repeat-screening city event.
213	- **Miami Art Week / Art Basel Miami Beach** (December; curated core + off —
214	  promoted from this page's unassessed tail 2026-09-01). One fixed week (2–9
215	  Dec in 2024) with **20+ art fairs and 1,200+ galleries in aggregate**
216	  scattered across Miami Beach, Wynwood, the Design District, Downtown and
217	  beyond; the anchor fair alone carried 280+ galleries with public day
218	  tickets at $85. Each fair is separately publicly ticketed and open daily
219	  through the week — sequencing, not triage — and metro traffic makes travel
220	  the binding constraint. The strongest non-theatre clear found:
221	  structurally a fringe whose shows are fairs.
222	- **Open House Festival, London** (September; a city-wide open week). **Over
223	  800 free open days and events across all 33 boroughs** in 9 days (12–20
224	  Sep 2026, 35th edition): drop-in for most buildings, per-item booked slots
225	  for the popular ones — free, but a real scarce-slot race (bookings open
226	  ~3.5 weeks out and the hot buildings go in minutes). Venue spread is the
227	  most extreme on this page. One caveat keeps it at the tier's edge: many
228	  buildings open on a single day of the nine, so part of the catalogue is
229	  triage rather than optimization (dimension 5, partial).
230	
231	### Near misses — one dimension short
232	
233	- **Milan — Salone del Mobile / Fuorisalone** (April; curated core + off). The
234	  purest non-theatre version of the Edinburgh dynamic: a ticketed trade fair at
235	  Rho with 1,900+ exhibitors, plus **1,100+ events listed on the official
236	  Fuorisalone guide (1,300+ across the city) spread over 16 districts** and
237	  **500,000+ visitors**. Brera alone carried 320 events across 217 showrooms.
238	  Installations run for the week rather than to performance times, so
239	  simultaneity (dimension 3) never bites: the *scheduling* problem is weaker
240	  than the *reachability* problem — which is the half of the product the Now
241	  page serves.
242	- **Charleston, SC — Spoleto Festival USA / Piccolo Spoleto** (late May–June;
243	  curated core + open companion). Piccolo Spoleto 2026 offered **250 events**,
244	  190 of them produced by independent arts and community groups, 113 free — a
245	  deliberately open companion to a curated core, at a scale where a planner is
246	  plausible but not urgent. Short of the bar on abundance (dimension 2).
247	- **Toronto, Canada** (30 Jun – 12 Jul 2026; lottery-selected fringe). **123
248	  shows**, selected by *lottery* rather than pure open access — a different
249	  supply mechanism, and small enough that overwhelm is not really the user's
250	  problem. Short on abundance (dimension 2).
251	- **Galway, Ireland — GIAF** (13–26 July 2026; curated season). Fourteen days,
252	  audiences well in excess of 200,000, in a small city fully consumed by it.
253	  Programme size unassessed — provisionally here until a show count is cited.
254	- **Israel's cinematheque festivals — Jerusalem, Docaviv (Tel Aviv), Haifa**
255	  (July / late May–June / the Sukkot holiday week; curated film festivals).
256	  All three clear seven dimensions: 8–11 day windows, 120–200+ films each
257	  screened 2–3 times, four to five parallel halls, open per-screening
258	  tickets at ₪43–49, and 28–43 year anchors in the same cities. What each
259	  misses is venue spread (dimension 4): everything concentrates in one
260	  cinematheque hub, so travel never binds and daily volume tops out near 28
261	  screenings — a planner is useful there, not indispensable. Detail and
262	  citations on [festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md)'s
263	  film adjacency, extended to Israel 2026-09-01.
264	- **Gen Con, Indianapolis** (July–Aug; convention — badge plus per-event
265	  tickets). The closest non-festival analogue found anywhere: **nearly
266	  30,000 unique ticketed events in four days** for ~72,000 attendees (2025,
267	  sold out), every event booked individually on top of a ~$155 badge with $2
268	  generic tickets as standby — the Fringe's model with a cover charge,
269	  anchored to Indianapolis since 2003 and contracted there through 2030.
270	  Event registration is itself a famous scarcity rush. What it misses: the
271	  window (4 days, dimension 1) and venue spread (one connected downtown
272	  campus — walking, not travel, is the constraint; dimension 4).
273	- **NYC Restaurant Week** (twice yearly; the reservation-as-ticket model).
274	  Nearly **600 restaurants across all five boroughs** on $30/$45/$60
275	  prix-fixe menus for four weeks (summer 2025), booked through OpenTable —
276	  a genuinely scarce per-item public slot that repeats daily through the
277	  window. Misses on intensity (dimension 3): two or three meal slots a day
278	  is planning, but rarely *conflict* — and the catalogue is the city's
279	  ordinary restaurant scene, already served by incumbent dining tools.
280	
281	### Fails the bar, instructively
282	
283	- **Salzburg, Austria** (17 Jul – 30 Aug 2026). **208 performances**
284	  announced for 2026; the delivered 2025 season was **174 performances over
285	  45 days at 16 venues, at 98.4% occupancy** — roughly four a day, so an
286	  evening rarely forecloses more than one alternative. The town is
287	  overwhelmed, but the programme is curated, expensive and near-sold-out — a
288	  season you *book*, not a schedule you optimize. The boundary case this
289	  page keeps on purpose: *city swarming* alone fails abundance and
290	  simultaneity (dimensions 2–3), even with the deepest anchor on this page
291	  (annual in one town since 1920).
292	- **Venice — Biennale Arte** (9 May – 22 Nov 2026). **100 national
293	  participations** — 29 in the Giardini, 25 in the Arsenale and **46 scattered
294	  across the city** — plus **31 collateral events**. A months-long run means
295	  opening hours, not performance times: fails time-boxing (1) and simultaneity
296	  (3) at once. **Kassel — Documenta** (every five years, 100 days) fails the
297	  cadence half of recurrence; the roving **Manifesta** fails the anchor half.
298	- **Cannes**, **SXSW Austin** (March). Both convert a city into temporary
299	  venues at high density with genuine clash-resolution problems, but both are
300	  trade/badge-driven rather than public-audience-driven — failing open access
301	  (dimension 6) — and SXSW already ships its own scheduling tool.
302	- **Fashion week — Paris, Milan, New York, London** (the owner's direct
303	  question, 2026-09-01). It has festival *shape*: a fixed week per city
304	  (NYFW's February 2026 official calendar ran 6 days with 60+ shows and
305	  presentations; Paris womenswear runs 9 days with ~68 shows and 33
306	  presentations), venues scattered across the city, twice-plus a year in
307	  the same capitals. It fails the bar twice over. **The real catalogue is
308	  invitation- and accreditation-only** — runway seats go to press, buyers
309	  and clients, and what the public can buy (Runway 7-style independent
310	  showcases in New York, London's £135 public-ticket experiment of 2019,
311	  Copenhagen's partly-open schedule) is a parallel shadow programme, not
312	  the shows that matter (dimension 6). And **every show happens exactly
313	  once** (dimension 5), so even for insiders it is triage, not
314	  optimization. The scheduling pain is real; the bookable market is absent.
315	- **The Summer Olympics** (the owner's other direct question; mega-event).
316	  Paris 2024 is the strongest possible showing for the shape: 17 days, **767
317	  ticketed sessions across 35 venues** (~20 in and around one city), **9.5
318	  million tickets sold** to the general public from €24, with an official
319	  face-value resale app — better-behaved public access than most festivals,
320	  plus genuine abundance and binding travel. It still fails the two
321	  dimensions a planning product compounds on: sessions never repeat (the
322	  100m final does not recur on Tuesday; dimension 5), and **the host city
323	  rotates every four years** (dimension 7), so venue data, travel matrices
324	  and source work are worthless at the next edition. A real planning
325	  market — for exactly one summer per city. FIFA World Cup 2026 doubles the
326	  failure: 104 matches across 16 cities in three countries, with flights as
327	  the travel legs.
328	- **The badge-and-queue worlds — San Diego Comic-Con, CES** (conventions).
329	  SDCC: ~130,000 attendees and dozens of parallel programming tracks, but
330	  **one badge and then first-come queueing** — no per-item slot exists to
331	  book (Hall H is famously camped overnight), so the optimization is real
332	  but unbookable (dimension 6), and its fan-run schedule guides are the
333	  community routing around that. CES: 4,100+ exhibitors across two Las
334	  Vegas campuses far enough apart that navigation is a product feature —
335	  but trade-only badges, closed to the public (dimension 6 again, from the
336	  other side).
337	- **Burning Man** (temporary city). Nine days, one rebuilt city, and a
338	  community-published catalogue of **4,300+ participant-run events** (the
339	  2018 Playa Events count) — proof that an event catalogue emerges wherever
340	  abundance meets a time box, even with no commerce at all. It fails on
341	  access (one $550+ ticket covers everything; per-event ticketing is
342	  unticketable by ideology; dimension 6) and on city context (dimension 8:
343	  there is no surrounding city — food and rest are things you truck in).
344	
345	### The unassessed tail
346	
347	The World Fringe network holds 300+ fringes worldwide (Perth's own materials
348	say 400+), and the tail is thin — only three sell more than 250,000 tickets.
349	In the network and unassessed here: **Prague**, **Dublin**, **Winnipeg**,
350	**Orlando**, **Minnesota**, **Wellington**, **Camden**, **Melbourne Fringe**.
351	
352	The cross-cutting finding from scoring the non-festival world (2026-09-01):
353	**open per-event access is the definition's rarest dimension.** Big
354	real-world events default to allocating scarcity by badge, invitation or
355	queue; genuinely bookable per-item inventory is what festivals proper, Gen
356	Con, the art fairs, Open House and restaurant weeks share. And it is the
357	pairing of that access with an annual anchor that makes a planning product's
358	data investment compound — where either half fails, the planning problem
359	still exists but belongs to insiders (fashion week, CES), queue-campers
360	(SDCC), or a single summer (each Olympics).
361	# City context sources — finding everything else that's on
362	
363	Where "what else is going on in this city" gets published, and how a product
364	can read it. This page exists on the owner's direction (2026-09-01): a
365	festival visitor also wants the rest of the city — other events that week,
366	attractions, markets — and the wiki's job is **not** to hold any particular
367	weekend's events but to hold **the sources**: which publications, feeds and
368	APIs carry a city's non-festival goings-on, per festival city, and how
369	machine-readable each is. Scoped to the cities of the longer festivals
370	([festival-circuits/](../festival-circuits/README.md)'s
371	fringe-shaped tier), not the weekend showcases. Edinburgh's own August
372	*festival* cluster is [edinburgh-festival-season/](../edinburgh-festival-season/README.md)'s;
373	this page is about everything those pages don't list. Compiled once, refined
374	in place.
375	
376	Every claim below was verified by direct fetch on 2026-09-01 unless marked
377	as a search-attributed claim; "closed" verdicts name what was actually
378	probed.
379	
380	## Key insights
381	
382	- Events listings are a per-country licensed market: Data Thistle (UK), ATDW (Australia), Eventfinda (NZ) cover our cities in one API each.
383	- Montreal is the outlier: the city's own open-data portal publishes its events calendar as CSV/GeoJSON, refreshed daily.
384	- Tourism-board sites have no APIs — but their event detail pages carry schema.org JSON-LD, so one parser covers every city.
385	- The open-API era is over: Eventbrite killed public event search in 2020, Songkick takes no new keys, Fever bought DICE.
386	- Ticketmaster Discovery and Skiddle are the free keyed baseline — geo-searchable, 5k calls/day, with a ticketed-music skew.
387	- Attractions are solved free: OSM Overpass plus Wikidata; Viator's no-gate affiliate tier adds bookable tours with commission.
388	- Data Thistle is competitor and supplier at once: it sells the listings feed the UK's own tourism boards run on.
389	
390	## The source classes
391	
392	**1. Tourism-board (DMO) event calendars** are the best human-curated
393	coverage of "everything else in town" — promoters submit events directly
394	(every DMO probed has a submit flow) — and the weakest machine surface: none
395	probed offers a documented API. The verified pattern across seven DMOs:
396	index pages carry only site-level JSON-LD, but **event detail pages carry
397	full schema.org `Event` markup** (wellingtonnz.com's detail pages have
398	`MusicEvent` with `startDate` and `Place`), so the generic integration is a
399	sitemap crawl plus a JSON-LD parse of detail pages — one parser for every
400	city. Some have undocumented JSON backends (aucklandnz.com calls its own
401	`/api/events/get`); some are bot-hostile (visitmelbourne.com 403s
402	non-browsers; What's On Melbourne renders client-side).
403	
404	**2. City open-data portals** carry attractions/POI and event
405	*infrastructure*, not live listings — with one exception worth building on:
406	[Montreal's "Événements publics" dataset](https://donnees.montreal.ca/)
407	(CKAN, API works unauthenticated) is the city's own calendar as
408	CSV/GeoJSON — date, event type, audience, cost, location — last modified
409	the day it was checked, i.e. maintained daily. Melbourne's Opendatasoft
410	portal (239 datasets, open API) has venues, landmarks and event *permits*
411	but no calendar; Edinburgh's legacy portal was unreachable (502) and its
412	live ArcGIS portal is spatial-only.
413	
414	**3. Commercial listings media** (Time Out, The Skinny, Broadsheet, The
415	List's consumer site) are editorial and scrape-only; no licensing program
416	surfaced for Time Out. The class that matters sits behind them:
417	
418	**4. Licensed events-data suppliers — the class the UK actually runs on.**
419	[Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/) (The List's data arm,
420	Edinburgh-based) claims over half a million future performances UK-wide and
421	publishes a [documented Publishing API](https://api.datathistle.com/) —
422	free registration, event/place/schedule/performance model **with
423	per-performance prices and booking links** — and its named clients include
424	VisitScotland, Visit Brighton, Visit Liverpool and Transport for Edinburgh,
425	via the Simpleview CMS the DMOs run on. One integration would cover
426	Edinburgh, Brighton and Leicester at once — and its data model is
427	structurally a superset of what EdFringeNow already stores. Australia's
428	equivalent is national and official: the
429	[Australian Tourism Data Warehouse ATLAS API](https://developer.atdw.com.au/)
430	(products *and events*, feeding the state DMO sites; distributor
431	registration A$660 once-off with a 30-day trial, per its own FAQ) — one
432	paid integration covers Melbourne and Adelaide. New Zealand's is
433	[Eventfinda's API](https://www.eventfinda.co.nz/api/v2/index) (free key by
434	application, display-only licence with attribution) covering Auckland and
435	Wellington.
436	
437	**5. Ticketing-platform discovery APIs** — the survivors and the dead:
438	[Ticketmaster Discovery](https://developer.ticketmaster.com/products-and-docs/apis/discovery-api/v2/)
439	(free key, 5,000 calls/day, geo+date+venue search, global) and
440	[Skiddle](https://github.com/Skiddle/web-api) (UK; free key, lat/long/radius,
441	event codes including COMEDY and EXHIB) are real and open.
442	**Eventbrite has no public discovery API** — the public event search was
443	removed in February 2020 and the API is org-scoped now; **Songkick** takes
444	no new API applications (commercial licence ~$500/month per its support
445	pages); **DICE** is partner-only and was acquired by **Fever** (itself
446	closed) in June 2025; **Bandsintown** is artist-scoped — the wrong shape
447	for city-wide discovery. Universe has an open GraphQL API but niche
448	inventory.
449	
450	**6. Event-intelligence aggregators**: [PredictHQ](https://docs.predicthq.com/)
451	sells exactly "all events in a city" (free tier exists; real pricing
452	negotiated) but is built for demand forecasting — whether its licence
453	permits consumer republishing is unverified and decides whether it is
454	usable at all. SeatGeek's Platform API is real, free-keyed, US-leaning.
455	
456	**7. Attractions, as distinct from events**: the free, licence-clean base
457	layer is [OpenStreetMap's Overpass API](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Overpass_API)
458	(`tourism=attraction|museum|viewpoint`, opening hours where mapped) joined
459	with [Wikidata's SPARQL endpoint](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:SPARQL_query_service)
460	(CC0 entities, coordinates, images, Wikipedia links) — the "free hour near
461	me" gazetteer, and the machine version of the hand-curated list
462	[edinburgh-festival-season/](../edinburgh-festival-season/README.md) said couldn't exist as a
463	feed. For *bookable* attractions,
464	[Viator's Partner API basic-access tier is free with no pre-authorization](https://docs.viator.com/partner-api/technical/)
465	(search, availability, pricing, commission on referred bookings) — which
466	also plugs into the affiliate lane
467	[competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md)'s revenue
468	analysis found empty among rivals; GetYourGuide gates its API behind 100k
469	monthly visits and Tiqets behind partner contact; Google Places is paid
470	per-request; Atlas Obscura is bot-blocked with no API.
471	
472	## Per-city: what a product would actually read
473	
474	| City (festival, window) | Best sources | Machine access |
475	|---|---|---|
476	| Edinburgh (Fringe, Aug) | Data Thistle API; The List editorial; Ticketmaster + Skiddle | documented API; scrape; APIs |
477	| Melbourne (MICF, Mar–Apr) | ATDW ATLAS API; What's On Melbourne; data.melbourne | paid API; headless scrape only; open API (POI, no listings) |
478	| Adelaide (Fringe, Feb–Mar) | ATDW (same integration); southaustralia.com (ATDW-powered) | paid API; detail-page scrape |
479	| Brighton (Fringe, May) | Data Thistle (VisitBrighton is its client); visitbrighton.com | same UK API; JSON-LD scrape |
480	| Montreal (JFL, Jul) | city open-data events dataset; mtl.org; Ticketmaster | CSV/GeoJSON, daily; JS site; API |
481	| Auckland + Wellington (NZICF, May) | Eventfinda API; DMO sites | free key + attribution; JSON-LD scrape |
482	| Leicester (comedy festival, Feb) | Data Thistle; visitleicester.info; Skiddle | same UK API; detail-page scrape; API |
483	
484	The synthesis the research supports: **three integrations cover the need at
485	lowest cost** — (1) one licensed listings API per country (Data Thistle /
486	ATDW / Eventfinda, with Montreal's open data replacing the class there),
487	(2) Ticketmaster Discovery + Skiddle as the free cross-city baseline, and
488	(3) OSM + Wikidata for attractions with Viator's affiliate tier when
489	bookable tours (and their commission) are wanted. The universal fallback
490	for any DMO without an API is the sitemap-crawl + `Event` JSON-LD parse.
491	Time Out, Eventbrite, Songkick, Fever/DICE and Atlas Obscura are closed for
492	this purpose and not worth integration effort.
493	
494	## Sources
495	
496	- [Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/) and the [Publishing API](https://api.datathistle.com/) — coverage claim, client list, data model with per-performance prices; fetched 2026-09-01.
497	- [ATDW — distributor registration and FAQ](https://atdw.com.au/) and the [ATLAS API documentation](https://developer.atdw.com.au/) — the A$660 registration and 30-day trial are ATDW's own stated terms.
498	- [Eventfinda API](https://www.eventfinda.co.nz/api/v2/index) and [its terms](https://www.eventfinda.co.nz/api/terms) — free key, display-only licence, attribution.
499	- [Ville de Montréal open data — package search](https://donnees.montreal.ca/) — the "Événements publics" dataset (CSV/GeoJSON/SHP), modified same-day at check.
500	- [Ticketmaster Discovery API](https://developer.ticketmaster.com/products-and-docs/apis/discovery-api/v2/) — free key, 5,000 calls/day, 5 req/sec defaults.
501	- [Skiddle web API (GitHub)](https://github.com/Skiddle/web-api) — free key by application; event codes including COMEDY and EXHIB.
502	- [Eventbrite platform docs](https://www.eventbrite.com/platform/docs/introduction) and the [public-search removal record (Automattic's eventbrite-api issue)](https://github.com/Automattic/eventbrite-api/issues/83) — no public discovery endpoint since Feb 2020.
503	- [Songkick API support page](https://support.songkick.com/hc/en-us/articles/360012423194) — closed to new applications; commercial licence pricing as stated there.
504	- [DICE partners](https://dice.fm/partners) and [Fever's acquisition of DICE (Fever newsroom)](https://newsroom.feverup.com/) — partner-only API; June 2025 acquisition.
505	- [Bandsintown artist API docs](https://artists.bandsintown.com/support/api) — artist-scoped access.
506	- [PredictHQ docs](https://docs.predicthq.com/) and [pricing page](https://www.predicthq.com/pricing) — plans self-reported; republishing terms unverified.
507	- [Viator Partner API — levels of access](https://partnerresources.viator.com/travel-commerce/levels-of-access/) and [technical docs](https://docs.viator.com/partner-api/technical/) — free basic affiliate tier, no pre-authorization.
508	- [GetYourGuide partner API gate](https://partner.getyourguide.support/hc/en-us/articles/13981133907613) — ≥100k monthly visits for Basic.
509	- [Overpass API (OSM wiki)](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Overpass_API) and [Wikidata SPARQL service](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:SPARQL_query_service).
510	- [Google Places web service](https://developers.google.com/maps/documentation/places/web-service/overview) — paid per-request; [Things to do is operator-side](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13189190).
511	- DMO probes, all fetched 2026-09-01: [wellingtonnz.com events](https://www.wellingtonnz.com/visit/events) (detail-page `MusicEvent` JSON-LD), [aucklandnz.com events](https://www.aucklandnz.com/events) (internal `/api/events/get`), [What's On Melbourne](https://whatson.melbourne.vic.gov.au/) (client-rendered), [visitmelbourne.com](https://www.visitmelbourne.com/) (403 to non-browsers), [data.melbourne explore API](https://data.melbourne.vic.gov.au/), [southaustralia.com](https://southaustralia.com/) (ATDW asset URLs), [visitbrighton.com](https://www.visitbrighton.com/whats-on/) (Simpleview CMS), [visitleicester.info](https://www.visitleicester.info/whats-on/), [edinburgh.org what's-on](https://edinburgh.org/whats-on/), [mtl.org](https://www.mtl.org/en/what-to-do/festivals-and-events), [lavitrine.com](https://www.lavitrine.com/) (JS SPA, no public API), [timeout.com/edinburgh](https://www.timeout.com/edinburgh), [list.co.uk](https://list.co.uk/), [atlasobscura.com](https://www.atlasobscura.com/) (403).
512	
513	## Open questions
514	
515	- **What does Data Thistle actually cost, and would its licence allow our
516	  static-file architecture?** Registration is free but commercial licensing
517	  is contact-priced — the same two questions
518	  [edinburgh-festival-season/](../edinburgh-festival-season/README.md) has open against the
519	  Edinburgh Festivals Listings API (redistribution vs our committed-JSON
520	  model), now against the UK-wide supplier too. One conversation covers
521	  both of its roles (supplier here, competitor on
522	  [competitor-landscape/](../competitor-landscape/README.md)).
523	- **Does Data Thistle's feed carry the Fringe itself at scrape-grade
524	  fidelity?** If its half-million UK performances include the full Fringe
525	  programme with prices, it is also a candidate *second source* for our
526	  core data — unexamined.
527	- **PredictHQ's republishing terms** — unverified, and they decide whether
528	  the category is usable for a consumer product at all.
529	- **How complete is DMO detail-page JSON-LD in practice?** The pattern is
530	  verified on single pages per site; nobody has measured what fraction of a
531	  DMO's events carry parseable markup.
532	- **Montreal's dataset boundary** — whether "Événements publics" covers
533	  only city-run events or the full cultural calendar (La Vitrine's
534	  aggregator ambitions suggest the private layer is separate and closed).
535	- **Edinburgh's own gap is real**: no UK open-data events feed, The List's
536	  consumer site is scrape-only, and the council portal was unreachable this
537	  pass — for our home city, Data Thistle or nothing is the current read.
538	- **ATDW's 30-day trial** is the cheap probe when Melbourne/Adelaide
539	  support becomes live — deferred to adoption time, like the circuit
540	  page's deep dives.
541	
542	## Growth log
543	
544	- **2026-09-01** — page created deliberately on the owner's direction
545	  ("where those are published and how we can find them" — sources, not
546	  events), from a verification-first research pass: the seven source
547	  classes with fetch-verified machine-readability verdicts, the
548	  per-country licensed-supplier finding (Data Thistle / ATDW / Eventfinda),
549	  Montreal's daily-refreshed open-data events calendar, the DMO
550	  detail-page JSON-LD pattern, the closed-API graveyard (Eventbrite,
551	  Songkick, Fever/DICE, Time Out, Atlas Obscura), the OSM+Wikidata
552	  attractions layer with Viator's free affiliate tier, and the per-city
553	  source table for the fringe-tier festival cities. All claims cited;
554	  integration choices left for humans.
555	# product-requirements
556	
557	The human-reviewed distillation of the research wikis into product requirements
558	for EdFringeNow. This is the **only** crossing point out of `product-wiki/`: the
559	rest of the repo may reference what lands here, and nothing else under
560	`product-wiki/`.
561	
562	Nothing is auto-grown here — entries are added by hand when a research finding is
563	reviewed and promoted into a requirement.
